Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 150 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2019) 
Background 
Alberta Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 150 (Jenner WMU) is found in the southeast of the province around the northern 
perimeter of Canadian Forces Base Suffield. It covers an area of approximately 1,828 km2. This area is within the dry 
mixedgrass natural subregion of the province. The WMU encompasses land west, north and east of Canadian Forces Base 
Suffield to Secondary Highway 555, which is the northern WMU border. The western extent of the WMU begins at Secondary 
Highway 884 south of Jenner, and extends east to the Alberta/Saskatchewan border. The southern boundary is road 
allowance 18-0 (Hilda road). The main habitat features within the WMU include the South Saskatchewan River valley as well 
as choppy sandhill complexes (Hilda Sandhills, Middle Sandhills). The primary land uses in the WMU are cattle grazing and 
annual crop production. Habitat consists of native grassland (the majority of which is Crown land), tame grassland, and 
cultivated cropland. Oil and gas development is also present, and in recent years, renewable energy development has 
increased within the WMU. Chronic Wasting disease is well established within the WMU, with an overall prevalence of 52.50% 
in 2019 and 64.15% in 2020 for mule deer bucks. A prevalence of 15.71% in 2019 and 28.57% in 2020 was documented in 
mule deer does from submitted samples. 
The established pre-hunting season population goal for WMU 150 is 1365 mule deer and 540 white-tailed deer. Ungulate 
harvest in WMU 150 is currently managed using a special license draw for antlered and antlerless mule deer, antlerless white-
tailed deer, elk, and moose. During the archery only season, white-tailed deer and mule deer are hunted with general licenses, 
which are available without the requirement of a Special License obtained through the draw process. Landowner licenses for 
mule deer and elk are also available to eligible residents. 
A comprehensive survey for mule deer was last conducted for WMU 150 in 2006 using a modified Gasaway methodology, 
thus results between 2014 and 2019 are not easily comparable. The survey resulted in an estimate of 581 mule deer. This 
survey occurred during depopulation efforts aimed at control of CWD spread, thus the WMU was significantly below goal at 
that time (Table 1). 
The objective of the February 2019 survey was to assess the status of the ungulate population in WMU 150 by determining 
estimates for abundance, density and age-sex composition. We also recorded observations of additional species of game 
management or conservation concern including elk, moose, pronghorn, carnivores, game birds, and sensitive or at risk 
species. 
Survey method 
A rotary wing transect survey was conducted February 12-13, 2019 flying 23 east-west lines at 1.85 km intervals, which 
obtained 42.7% coverage (800 m wide survey strip, area surveyed 781.3 km2). At each observation point, ungulates were 
classified by species, and when possible, sex and age was recorded. Antler size for bucks was classified as ‘small’ (spike or 
two points on one or both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or more points; antlers inside ears), or large (antlers with ≥ 4 
points, antlers outside of ears). 
Elk and moose observations made during the survey were also recorded, though population estimates were not calculated as 
the survey method and sample obtained was not appropriate for these species. 
Results 
A total of 553 mule deer were observed with an average groups size of 13 (range 1-45). The estimated density was 0.71 mule 
deer/km2 and the estimated abundance was 1294 individuals, representing a 222% increase in mule deer abundance since 
the Gasaway survey in 2006. However these results are not readily comparable due to differing methodology. A total of 447

mule deer were successfully classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 75:100:61. That results in an 
estimated 2019 winter mule deer population of 411 bucks, 547 does, and 336 fawns. Of the 142 mule deer bucks classified, 39 
(27.5%) were classified ‘small’, 47 (33.1%) ‘medium’, and 56 (39.4%) ‘large’. 
A total of 142 white-tailed deer were observed with an average group size of 14 (range 1-35). The estimated density was 0.18 
deer/km2 and the estimated abundance was 332 individuals. White-tailed deer population estimates were not available from 
2006 data. A total of 107 white-tailed deer were successfully classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 
2:100:60. That results in an estimated 2019 early winter white-tailed deer population of three bucks, 205 does, and 124 fawns. 
The one white-tailed deer buck that was classified was ‘large’. Based on these results, it is certain that white-tail antler shed 
had already occurred, and age-sex ratios should be interpreted with caution, and are undoubtedly inaccurate due to the 
inability to distinguish shed bucks from does. 
A supplemental survey of the adjacent Red Deer River valley in WMU’s 150 and 151 was also conducted as part of the 
combined WMU 150 and WMU 732 elk census. A total of 21 moose were observed during this aerial survey. These 
observations were not suitable to estimate population, however, the result indicates there is a low density of moose within 
WMU 150 with the exception of a small area of the river valley. Seven elk and 1,204 pronghorn were also counted during the 
WMU 150 survey. Other species observed included, sharp-tailed grouse, bald eagle, coyote, and Hungarian partridge.
